e-6641.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Step Functions
e-6641.problem: Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s) = \mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ for $f(t) = u(t - 2) + u(t-6),$ where $u$ is the unit step function.
e-6641.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise functions $u(t-2)$ and $u(t-6),$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-2) & ={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<2 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 2\end{aligned} \\ u(t-6) & ={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<6 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 6.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14043349/assets/6ddb2983dec1f3221778a336bb6ef3cce3138476b67d64334ab6660184a79f95.png)

So, for our Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{6}1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the second integral diverges for $s \leq 0.$

For $s > 0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{6}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s}]}_{2}^{6}+2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{6}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-6s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}-\frac{2}{s}(0-{e}^{-6s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}+\frac{2{e}^{-6s}}{s} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} =\dfrac{e^{-2s}}{s} +\dfrac{e^{-6s}}{s}, 
\qquad 
s > 0.
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find $L{f(t)}$ for the piecewise function defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<1 \\ -7,\, & 1\le t\le 3 \\ 0,\, & t>3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)={\begin{aligned}0\, & \text{for}\,\,t<1 \\ -7\, & \text{for}\,\,1\le t\le 3 \\ 0\, & \text{for}\,\,t>3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t={\int }_{1}^{3}(-7){e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate this definite integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(-7){e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{7}{s}{e}^{-st}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{s}({e}^{-3s}-{e}^{-s})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
L{f(t)}=\frac{7}{s}({e}^{-3s}-{e}^{-s}).
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Step Functions
content.problem:
Find $L{f(t)}$ for the piecewise function defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<1 \\ -7,\, & 1\le t\le 3 \\ 0,\, & t>3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)={\begin{aligned}0\, & \text{for}\,\,t<1 \\ -7\, & \text{for}\,\,1\le t\le 3 \\ 0\, & \text{for}\,\,t>3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t={\int }_{1}^{3}(-7){e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate this definite integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(-7){e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{7}{s}{e}^{-st}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{s}({e}^{-3s}-{e}^{-s})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
L{f(t)}=\frac{7}{s}({e}^{-3s}-{e}^{-s}).
$$

decision.explanation: For t≥0, u(5-t) equals 1 up to t=5 and 0 afterward. Thus F(s)=\int_0^5 e^{-st}\,dt=\frac{1}{s}(1-e^{-5s}) for s>0.

after.problem: Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)}$ for $s>0,$ where $f(t)=u(5-t)$ and $u$ is the unit step function.$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}}
after.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(5-t)={\begin{aligned}1,\, & t\le 5 \\ 0,\, & t>5\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }u(5-t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We compute this integral for $s>0$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s}]}_{0}^{5} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s}(1-{e}^{-5s})\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Step Functions
content.problem: Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)}$ for $s>0,$ where $f(t)=u(5-t)$ and $u$ is the unit step function.$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}}
content.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(5-t)={\begin{aligned}1,\, & t\le 5 \\ 0,\, & t>5\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }u(5-t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We compute this integral for $s>0$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s}]}_{0}^{5} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s}(1-{e}^{-5s})\end{aligned}
$$
